text:
The largest gap in AI is no longer even between the US and China. It is between what is happening inside frontier labs and people still planning school, careers and life as if the old world will continue. We have the news, but no shared world model. Here is the map:

Most people underestimate the transition because everyday life has not changed dramatically yet. Schools are open, salaries arrive, degrees are awarded, traffic moves. But technological breaks accumulate first in labs and infrastructure; their social effects arrive later and often more abruptly.

That delay is not evidence of weak capability. It is diffusion and institutional latency. Electricity, the internet and computers did not transform the whole economy on the day they appeared. Today there are several generations between frontier systems and the average company, agency or free user.

In Notion’s survey of 6,118 professionals, 88% of organizations were still in the early stages of AI transformation. Only 2% had made AI part of the operating system of the organization. The finding says less about weak technology than about institutions that have not absorbed it.

Two opposite statements can therefore be true: AI has reached extraordinary levels in some tasks, while most organizations still use it for summaries, drafts and brainstorming. Measuring the frontier through average office usage is like judging a jet engine by urban traffic speed.

Free ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok and a basic corporate bot are discussed under the same label as long-horizon agents. Yet one is an interface that answers; the other writes code, operates terminals, tests through browsers, conducts research and delegates work to other agents.

Anthropic’s Fable 5 and the more restricted Mythos 5 symbolize the gap. Fable is a safeguarded Mythos-class model released for broad use; Mythos is powerful enough in areas such as cybersecurity to trigger debates over trusted access, state review and export controls.

OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol is not merely a better conversational model either. It pushes the frontier on long command-line workflows, scientific analysis and cybersecurity; its ultra mode coordinates subagents on the same task, moving beyond the capability of a single agent.

Sakana AI’s Fugu and Fugu Ultra point in another direction: rather than trusting one model, an orchestration model dynamically selects and coordinates specialists for the task. Behind one API, learned Thinker, Worker and Verifier roles can be assigned across a model pool.

OpenRouter’s Fusion reaches a similar destination through a different design. A panel of models studies the same problem in parallel; a judge synthesizes consensus, contradictions, blind spots and unique findings. On some research tasks, panels of budget models can beat individual frontier models.

The larger lesson is more important than the model names: the strongest system is not always the strongest single model. Routing, diversity, parallel research, critique and synthesis add system intelligence on top of raw model intelligence.

This is why harness engineering is becoming a central discipline. A harness determines how the model plans, which tools it calls, how it manages context, what it may change, how it tests outputs and how it recovers when something fails.

An agent is not just a long prompt. It is a loop: plan, act, observe, test, critique, repair and try again. In production, the decisive capability is not the brilliance of the first answer, but whether the system can detect failure and recover reliably.

Coding has become the most visible laboratory of the transition. New agents can read repositories, infer architecture, edit files, run tests, inspect the product through a browser and try another approach after failure. Humans are moving from writing every line toward designing goals and loops.

I see this directly in engineering and OSINT workflows: some research, prototyping, debugging and verification work I would once have expected to take six months can now be compressed into a single day with the right agentic workflow. Most people are not yet aware of how radically their own potential output has changed. But a powerful model is not enough; bad context and weak evaluations only produce mistakes at higher speed.

Andrew Ng’s three loops are useful here: the agentic engineering loop operating in minutes, developer feedback operating in hours, and external feedback from the real world arriving over days or weeks. As the first loop accelerates, human work moves upward.

For now, the strongest human advantage is often context. We know what the user actually wants, which trade-offs are acceptable, which metric creates fake success and why the product exists. A model can generate methods; choosing purposes and meaning remains harder.

An AI-native organization is not one that distributes chatbot licenses. It redesigns processes so machines can read, execute, measure and audit them. APIs, permissions, data quality, logs and evaluations are foundational infrastructure.

The leader-worker gap in Notion’s research also matters. Executives are far more likely than employees to say the organization is ready to deploy agents. Management may mistake purchased tools for transformation; operators see missing integrations, fragmented data and unreliable outputs.

Society fails to feel the transition because these layers move at different speeds. A frontier system may compress weeks of work into hours while most job descriptions, school programs and public services remain unchanged. Delayed visibility does not mean the underlying accumulation has stopped.

People are still choosing degrees, professions and thirty-year career paths under pre-AGI assumptions. That is understandable because institutions offer no alternative map. But betting that the next decade will resemble the present is becoming increasingly risky.

Education systems are amplifying the risk. Memorization, standardized tests and single-answer teaching do not prepare people for systems that continuously search, use tools and synthesize. Logic, scientific method, epistemology, source verification and AI literacy should be core subjects.

Media usually reports the transition as isolated events: a new model, investment, data center, chip restriction or benchmark record. Most stories may be accurate; but without a shared model connecting them, people cannot see the direction.

In one week you can read separate stories about Fable 5, Mythos, GPT-5.6 Sol, Fugu, Fusion, Chinese model-access controls and the UN dialogue on AI governance. Analyses that connect them as technical, economic and geopolitical layers of the same transition do exist, but they rarely reach broad audiences and their impact remains limited.

Social media makes this worse. Instagram, X, TikTok and YouTube rank content by its ability to hold attention, not by historical or strategic importance. A development that may change the balance of global power can disappear beneath celebrity drama or a short video optimized for outrage.

This problem is visible across the world: attention is locked into daily party politics, sports, crime, traffic accidents and celebrity cycles. None is entirely irrelevant, but the mental space devoted to the transition that may reshape production, employment, security and state capacity is tiny.

The public therefore appears informed while receiving only fragments. People see hundreds of headlines but cannot build causal links between them. Information abundance does not create meaning abundance; it can make the most consequential developments harder to see.

Explaining this is not doomerism. Calling everything an imminent paradise is boosterism; hiding risk and power concentration is marketing. A realist position takes the capability curve seriously while keeping uncertainty, bottlenecks and political choices in view.

The employment debate cannot be contained by the old cliché that some jobs disappear and new ones appear. If the marginal cost of cognitive labor keeps falling, the question is not only how occupations change, but where and for how long human labor remains economically competitive.

We do not have a strong basis for declaring mass unemployment impossible. The physical world, law, trust, robotics and institutional delay may slow displacement; they do not guarantee permanent protection. Substitution in white-collar work may move differently from earlier automation waves.

The deeper problem is not merely finding jobs. Taxation, pensions, social insurance, education, wage bargaining, corporate ownership and political representation were built around human labor at the center of the economy. If labor moves away from the center, institutions will not discover fairness automatically.

A productivity explosion could create abundance, but if chips, energy, models and distribution remain concentrated, abundance can also intensify power concentration. A post-labor economy may be technically possible without being politically stable or free.

The scientific upside is extraordinary. AI systems are combining literature review, hypothesis generation, coding, experimental design, simulation, data analysis and writing in a single loop. Before replacing the scientist overnight, they are increasing the clock speed of the laboratory.

Sakana’s AI Scientist built an end-to-end pipeline from idea generation through experiments, paper writing and review. Its new Nature-published stage is a real milestone, while methodological errors, hallucinations and weak scientific judgment remain real limitations.

The Darwin Gödel Machine, ShinkaEvolve and related systems show another threshold. One modifies its own harness code and measures the result; another uses LLM-driven program evolution to search for better algorithms. AI is becoming an active subject of AI engineering, not only its object.

A major AI contribution to a Nobel-level discovery in the near term would not be surprising. The more important threshold is when humans mostly choose the problem while systems routinely conduct most hypothesis generation, experimentation, analysis and verification.

Biology, materials science, energy, mathematics and physics are pivotal. Better batteries, catalysts, proteins, alloys, cooling or manufacturing methods can reduce compute and energy bottlenecks. More intelligence can accelerate the physical world, not only software.

Recursive self-improvement does not require an AI to “wake up” overnight. A concrete loop is simpler: the system improves its tools, code, experimental infrastructure or agent architecture; the improved system conducts better AI research; the next cycle accelerates.

Anthropic’s internal evidence says AI is already accelerating AI development. Its engineers now ship eight times as much code per quarter as in the earlier period, and agents can delegate hours of work to other agents. Fully autonomous successor design is not here, but the direction is visible.

As Lilian Weng argues, the first practical stage of RSI may happen in the harness before model weights. Better tool selection, memory, parallel agents, workflows, permissions, evaluations and persistent state can extract far more system intelligence from the same base model.

The Darwin Gödel Machine is a working early example: an agent changes its own execution code, adds tools and validation steps, then measures whether performance actually improves. It is not full RSI, but self-improvement is no longer only a theoretical diagram.

ShinkaEvolve evolves not only solutions but methods for producing solutions. Its ability to improve a loss function used in mixture-of-experts training matters because the feedback loop begins to touch the efficiency of training the next generation of models.

Google DeepMind’s From AGI to ASI report studies four paths together: scaling, paradigm shifts, recursive improvement and superintelligence emerging from large multi-agent collectives. These paths are not alternatives; they may accelerate one another.

The possibility of an intelligence explosion comes from compound feedback. Coding accelerates, research becomes cheaper, algorithms improve, chip design is optimized and science reduces energy or materials constraints. If several loops reinforce one another, the curve need not stay linear.

None of this is guaranteed or frictionless. Compute, energy, data, physical experiment time, supply chains, human approval and institutional coordination can create bottlenecks. Even a vastly smarter system cannot observe ten years of drug effects overnight.

Evaluation may be one of the central bottlenecks. A system can optimize the test instead of the real goal, hack the reward, fabricate logs or persuade the model auditing it. As autonomy grows, independent verifiers and security layers must grow with it.

Today’s frontier capability may become tomorrow’s local model. When systems near the level of Fable, GPT-5.6 Sol or their successors run on personal devices and private servers, privacy, cost, latency and technological autonomy change at once.

The geopolitical stack is larger than the model: chips, energy, data centers, cooling, model weights, training data, synthetic data, inference infrastructure, agent harnesses, evaluation sets, researchers and distribution channels together form strategic capacity.

This is why the chip war remains central. Chinese firms are reducing dependence on Nvidia through Huawei, Alibaba, Baidu and custom silicon; DeepSeek is developing its own inference chip. US labs are also pursuing custom hardware for cost, supply control and sovereignty.

US export controls were designed to slow China, but they also accelerated domestic chips, open models and alternative infrastructure. DeepSeek, GLM, MiniMax and MiMo ecosystems are no longer merely cheap followers; they generate strategic power through adoption, cost and open distribution.

Beijing’s discussion of restricting overseas access to China’s most advanced models is a clear sign of the new era. There is no final uniform policy yet, but criminalizing model leakage and keeping the strongest systems domestic are now being considered.

Washington has crossed the same threshold. Foreign access to Anthropic’s Fable 5 and Mythos 5 was briefly halted and later relaxed with new safeguards. A model release can now enter a state security process before it becomes an ordinary commercial launch.

The Fable-Mythos episode showed that frontier access can disappear overnight, affecting foreign staff, researchers, companies and countries. Model dependency is no longer only vendor lock-in; it is geopolitical and legal exposure.

Model sovereignty is therefore broader than building a national chatbot. It requires replaceable providers, local inference, open-weight options, ownership of logs, independent evaluations, data portability and emergency fallback models for critical missions.

Frontier labs are no longer ordinary technology companies. They are simultaneously economic actors, research institutions, critical infrastructure providers and geopolitical players. A company’s usage policy can directly affect a state’s cyber, intelligence or military capacity.

This creates a problem of decision sovereignty. When a state depends on a private model for critical systems, model versions, access policies, safety filters and the company’s ethical boundaries enter the national chain of command. Final human authority and model replaceability become architectural requirements.

Cybersecurity is the clearest dual-use domain. The same model can find vulnerabilities across millions of lines and develop patches, or help an attacker choose targets, generate exploits and scale operations. The line between tool and weapon increasingly depends on the user and context.

GPT-5.6 Sol competing with Mythos Preview on cyber evaluations, Fable 5’s safety classifiers and Mythos’s restricted distribution express the same tension: defenders need powerful tools, while the same capability creates systemic risk in malicious hands.

The use of advanced models by agencies such as CISA to audit public code illustrates the defensive side. Fear that the same class of systems could be used by foreign intelligence drives export controls. Cybersecurity may be approaching its own Stockfish moment.

Autonomous weapons and mass surveillance are not theoretical either. A lab’s boundary—“we will not support this”—can collide with a government’s demand for every lawful capability. The question is not only procurement; it is democratic legitimacy over lethal force.

The worst answer is to leave safety entirely to corporate conscience or secret state decisions. Companies lack democratic mandates; governments do not always have technical competence or transparency. Independent testing, incident reporting and a visible chain of accountability are necessary.

US-China competition is no longer a conventional trade war. Chips, models, data, energy, standards, cloud, researcher mobility and security policy are merging into one strategic contest. The same two powers constraining each other must also negotiate global AI governance.

Europe is trying to exercise power through law, market access and democratic standards. If the Global South becomes only a rule-taker, data supplier and renter of foreign models, a new digital dependency emerges. Access, language and local capacity are governance issues.

The UN’s first Global Dialogue on AI Governance matters for this reason. It is not a binding world government; it is an attempt to keep governments, companies, academia, civil society and the technical community inside a permanent channel of negotiation.

The first objective of global governance should not be one identical law. Shared evaluation language, incident reporting, model provenance, audit logs, cyber thresholds, accountability and cross-border liability are more realistic starting points. Systems may differ, but they must be measurable.

Governance is not the enemy of innovation. Aviation, medicine and nuclear energy earned trust through testing, standards, accountability and accident investigation—not by assuming markets would solve every failure. The danger is not regulation, but technically obsolete regulation.

Bureaucratic speed is also a sovereignty issue. Governments operate through annual plans, slow procurement, closed databases and fragmented agencies while model generations change within months. Slowness is not always prudence; sometimes it transfers capacity and decision-making to others.

At the individual level, the required skill is much broader than prompting: problem decomposition, systems design, source verification, data literacy, security, logic, philosophy and tool orchestration. AI literacy is the computer literacy of the new era.

Companies should map processes, build reusable evaluations, reduce dependence on one model and place human approvals according to risk. They should measure not whether AI was purchased, but which loops close and which outputs can be independently verified.

States need integrated capacity plans for compute, energy, education, cybersecurity, open research, data infrastructure and social policy. An AI strategy is not merely a subsidy package or regulatory text; it is the joint redesign of industry, science, security and the welfare state.

Universities must stop acting as credential factories. Curricula are aging before students graduate. Academia should preserve research quality, meaning, critical thought, original problem selection and public responsibility within increasingly automated knowledge production.

A practical rule for founders and engineers: measure the closed loop, not the model demo. Does the system receive real-world data, detect mistakes, repair them, know its cost, limit its authority and prove success independently? That is where durable value is created.

No single model name will define the next period. Fable, Mythos, GPT-5.6 Sol, Fugu, Fusion, GLM or tomorrow’s system will change. The durable question is how intelligence is orchestrated, who controls it, and how economic value and political power are distributed.

This transition is not merely technical, economic or geopolitical. It is simultaneously a reconstruction of science, labor, education, media, security, energy, state capacity and the human role in society. Watching the pieces separately makes us miss the whole.

The window is still open, but not at the pace institutions are used to. The answer is neither panic nor denial: learn, synthesize, measure, build, govern and adapt. We will either develop capacity during this transition or live under the conditions of systems built by others.
